trivia: Pepper says he learned of the session only on the morning it took place and had never met Miles Davis's rhythm section, yet the record is considered a milestone of his career. The liner notes and his memoir disagree on how long he had been away from the saxophone.

track.title: You'd Be So Nice to Come Home To
track.album: Art Pepper Meets the Rhythm Section
track.query: Art Pepper You'd Be So Nice to Come Home To Art Pepper Meets the Rhythm Section 1957
track.notes: Contemporary master of 19 Jan 1957, opening track of Art Pepper Meets the Rhythm Section (5:25); not Pepper's later remakes or the Rita Reys 1956 vocal

notes: Date, personnel and catalogue number from jazzdisco (Contemporary's studio, Los Angeles); the session story, the "milestone" verdict and the two accounts (two weeks per the liner notes, six months per the memoir "Straight Life") are from Wikipedia. A west-coast leader with an East Coast rhythm section, so west-coast is the closest style.

title: I Remember Clifford
original_issue: Blue Note BLP 1557 (LP "Lee Morgan Vol. 3", 1957)
personnel: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Gigi Gryce (alto sax), Benny Golson (tenor sax), Wynton Kelly (piano), Paul Chambers (bass), Charlie Persip (drums)
trivia: Benny Golson wrote this ballad for Clifford Brown, who died at 25, and Morgan was only 18 on the day he played the melody; Golson composed and arranged everything on the LP. Donald Byrd and Gigi Gryce had made the first recording of the tune in February 1957.

track.title: I Remember Clifford
track.query: Lee Morgan I Remember Clifford Lee Morgan Vol. 3 1957
track.notes: Blue Note take 5 of 24 Mar 1957 (7:07 on BLP 1557); not the first recording by Donald Byrd and Gigi Gryce (Jazz Lab, Feb 1957) or other later versions

notes: Date, take and personnel from jazzdisco (Van Gelder Studio, Hackensack); duration, the all-Golson repertoire and the Byrd/Gryce first recording from Wikipedia. Morgan was born 10 July 1938 (Wikipedia), so he was 18 at the session. Chosen over Candy (1957-11) to pair thematically with the Clifford Brown card.

title: Well, You Needn't
original_issue: Riverside RLP 12-242 (LP "Monk's Music", November 1957)
personnel: Thelonious Monk (piano), Ray Copeland (trumpet), Gigi Gryce (alto sax), Coleman Hawkins (tenor sax), John Coltrane (tenor sax), Wilbur Ware (bass), Art Blakey (drums)
trivia: Monk can be heard calling out for John Coltrane, then newly in his band, to take the first horn solo of this eleven-minute reading. Monk's Music is the only record on which Coleman Hawkins and Art Blakey played together.

track.title: Well, You Needn't
track.query: Thelonious Monk Septet Well You Needn't Monk's Music 1957
track.notes: Studio master from the Monk's Music LP (11:24); not Monk's earlier Blue Note versions or later live remakes

notes: The session ran 25 and 26 June 1957 at Reeves Sound Studios (jazzdisco and Wikipedia infobox; Wikipedia's lead says 26 June) and the day of this track is not given, so the month is used. The assignment named Straight, No Chaser or Ruby, My Dear with Coltrane, but neither fits: the 1957 Straight, No Chaser is the Gerry Mulligan session, the Monk's Music Ruby, My Dear is Monk with Hawkins (no Coltrane), and the Coltrane quartet Ruby, My Dear (July 1957) was first issued on Jazzland in 1961. Well, You Needn't is the Coltrane track with a clean 1957 release; Monk's Music is in the Grammy Hall of Fame (2001) per Wikipedia.

title: Li'l Darlin'
original_issue: Roulette LP "Basie" (also known as "The Atomic Mr. Basie" or "E=MC2"), first Basie album on Roulette, January 1958 per Wikipedia; catalogue number not verified
personnel: Count Basie (piano); trumpets Wendell Culley, Snooky Young, Thad Jones, Joe Newman; trombones Henry Coker, Al Grey, Benny Powell; reeds Marshal Royal, Frank Wess, Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis, Frank Foster, Charles Fowlkes; Freddie Green (guitar), Eddie Jones (bass), Sonny Payne (drums); arranger Neal Hefti
trivia: Neal Hefti's chart is praised by jazz writers for the way it swings at a very slow tempo. The Basie arrangement without lyrics was often used as the closing theme of "The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson".

track.title: Li'l Darlin'
track.query: Count Basie Li'l Darlin' The Atomic Mr. Basie 1957
track.notes: Basie orchestra's original 1957 Roulette studio recording, last track of the original LP (4:47); not the later vocal versions with lyrics or the small-group and guitar covers

notes: Wikipedia gives 21-22 October 1957 (Capitol studio, New York) for the album tracks without saying which day this one was cut, so the month is used; the LP appeared in 1958 (infobox: January 1958). The track-length and personnel are from the album page (Joe Williams sang only on a bonus track). The Roulette catalogue number was not verified, so the issue line omits it.

title: Haitian Fight Song
original_issue: Atlantic LP 1260 (LP "The Clown", September 1957); matrix 2458
personnel: Charles Mingus (bass), Jimmy Knepper (trombone), Shafi Hadi (alto and tenor sax; listed by jazzdisco under his birth name Curtis Porter), Wade Legge (piano), Dannie Richmond (drums)
trivia: Mingus said his bass solo here comes from thinking about prejudice and persecution but also carries determination. He chose the four tracks of "The Clown" partly to answer critics who said his music did not swing.

track.title: Haitian Fight Song
track.query: Charles Mingus Haitian Fight Song The Clown 1957
track.notes: Atlantic studio master of 12 Mar 1957, opening track of The Clown (12:01); not later versions by other groups

notes: Date, matrix 2458 and issue from jazzdisco (NYC, 12 Mar 1957); Wikipedia gives 13 Feb and 12 Mar 1957 for the album, 12:01 for the track and Hadi in the saxophone chair (he was born William Curtis Porter). The Mingus quotes are Mingus's own liner-note comments as reproduced on Wikipedia, paraphrased here. The assignment named Pithecanthropus Erectus (Jan 1956) for the Mingus slot; this track replaces it for recognisability (the best YouTube upload of Pithecanthropus Erectus has about 100k views against about 370k for Haitian Fight Song). Tier B is borderline: a Mingus-fan favourite rather than a general-audience tune.

title: Cool Struttin'
original_issue: Blue Note BLP 1588 (LP "Cool Struttin'", August 1958); 45 rpm Blue Note 45-1714 ("Cool Struttin' Parts 1 & 2", 1958)
personnel: Art Farmer (trumpet), Jackie McLean (alto sax), Sonny Clark (piano), Paul Chambers (bass), Philly Joe Jones (drums)
trivia: Clark's title track was played by a quintet whose rhythm team, Paul Chambers and Philly Joe Jones, came straight from Miles Davis's band. The sleeve photograph by Francis Wolff shows Alfred Lion's wife, Ruth.

track.title: Cool Struttin'
track.query: Sonny Clark Cool Struttin' Cool Struttin' 1958
track.notes: Blue Note master take 2 of the title track from 5 Jan 1958 (9:23 on the LP); not the Christmas-themed 1991 "Yule Struttin'" CD or later covers

notes: Date, take number, personnel and issues from jazzdisco (Van Gelder Studio, Hackensack); Wikipedia gives the same date, the August 1958 release and the 9:23 length. A YouTube search for the plain query returns full-album uploads first, but the "Cool Struttin' (Remastered)" Topic upload of the title track is among the top hits.

title: The Sermon!
original_issue: Blue Note BLP 4011 (LP "The Sermon!", 1959); 45 rpm Blue Note 45-1879 ("The Sermon Parts 1 & 2", 1959)
personnel: Jimmy Smith (organ), Lee Morgan (trumpet), Lou Donaldson (alto sax), Tina Brooks (tenor sax), Kenny Burrell (guitar), Art Blakey (drums)
trivia: This 20-minute Hammond organ blues was cut at the Manhattan Towers hotel ballroom in New York, which Rudy Van Gelder used as an extra studio for larger groups. Blue Note also issued it as a two-part 45 rpm single.

track.title: The Sermon!
track.query: Jimmy Smith The Sermon! The Sermon! 1958
track.notes: The Feb 1958 sextet take 15 (20:12 on the LP), not Smith's 1963 Verve remake with Kenny Burrell or the 1965 live version

notes: Date, take 15, personnel and issue numbers from jazzdisco (Manhattan Towers, New York); Wikipedia confirms the 25 Feb 1958 date for this track and the 20:12 length. The LP also holds tracks from a separate 25 Aug 1957 session (with George Coleman on alto), which are not the title track. Wikipedia dates the album release 1959 (December); jazzdisco lists both LP and single as 1959. The recording is about 21 months before release, so no gap flag.

title: Peter Gunn
original_issue: RCA Victor LPM-1956 mono / LSP-1956 stereo (LP "The Music from Peter Gunn", January 1959); also an RCA Victor single, January 1959 (b/w "The Brothers Go to Mother's"; catalogue number not found)
personnel: Henry Mancini (composer, conductor); John Williams (piano, the opening riff); Los Angeles studio players on the album include Pete Candoli and Conrad Gozzo (trumpet), Ted Nash and Plas Johnson (reeds), Bob Bain and Al Hendrickson (guitar), Rolly Bundock (bass), Shelly Manne (drums); the line-up varies from track to track
trivia: In his autobiography Mancini said the theme owes more to rock and roll than to jazz: one chord throughout, with piano and guitar playing an ostinato in unison. The album it opens won the first Grammy for Album of the Year.

track.title: Peter Gunn
track.query: Henry Mancini Peter Gunn The Music from Peter Gunn 1958
track.notes: Mancini's RCA Victor original from the soundtrack LP (2:06), not Ray Anthony's 1959 Capitol hit, Duane Eddy's cover or the Art of Noise remake

notes: The album sessions were 26 and 31 Aug and 4 and 29 Sep 1958 at Radio Recorders, Hollywood (Wikipedia); which day the theme was cut is not stated, so only the year is given. Wikipedia says the musicians vary by track, so the personnel line is the album roster plus the one track-specific credit it gives (John Williams on the piano riff, later a famous film composer); which horn players are on the theme itself is not documented. Length is 2:06 on the LP track list (the song page infobox says 2:04). Single and LP both January 1959 per Wikipedia; the single's catalogue number was not found. Grammy Hall of Fame has the track (2005) and the album (1998); the album is also in the National Recording Registry (2010). Tier A: widely known TV theme.

title: Peace Piece
original_issue: Riverside RLP 12-291 / RLP 1129 (LP "Everybody Digs Bill Evans", March 1959)
personnel: Bill Evans (piano, solo)
trivia: Evans improvised this meditation at the end of the session over a two-chord ostinato he had already used for "Some Other Time", and a trace of it returns in the opening of "Flamenco Sketches" on Kind of Blue. He refused requests to play it live in his last years, and is said to have performed it in public only once, with a dance company in Seattle in 1978.

track.title: Peace Piece
track.query: Bill Evans Peace Piece Everybody Digs Bill Evans 1958
track.notes: Solo piano studio recording from the 15 Dec 1958 session (6:37 on the LP); not Evans's later live or trio versions

notes: Date, studio (Reeves Sound, New York) and issue numbers from jazzdisco; release March 1959, track length and the solo status from Wikipedia (the album page's by-track bass and drums credits do not line up with its own track numbers, but jazzdisco's credits and the page text agree the piece is solo). The trivia about the 1978 performance is Wikipedia's claim that he played it live only once. Bill Evans may reach three cards in the whole set if a "Waltz for Debby" card exists, counting the joint Tony Bennett and Bill Evans card.

title: Blues Walk
original_issue: Blue Note BLP 1593 (LP "Blues Walk", 1958); 45 rpm Blue Note 45-1720 (b/w "The Masquerade Is Over", 1958)
personnel: Lou Donaldson (alto sax), Herman Foster (piano), Peck Morrison (bass), Dave Bailey (drums), Ray Barretto (congas)
trivia: Ray Barretto adds congas to Donaldson's group on this blues, the title track of an album that AllMusic's Steve Huey rates as the saxophonist's masterpiece. Donaldson remade the tune for Blue Note in December 1972.

track.title: Blues Walk
track.query: Lou Donaldson Blues Walk Blues Walk 1958
track.notes: Blue Note take 15 from 28 Jul 1958 (6:44 on the LP), not the 1972 remake on Sophisticated Lou

notes: Date, take 15, personnel and issues (BLP 1593; 45-1720) from jazzdisco (Van Gelder Studio, Hackensack); the 6:44 length, the 1958 release and the AllMusic judgement from Wikipedia's album page. The 1972 remake is jazzdisco's Sophisticated Lou session (11 Dec 1972, Blue Note BN-LA024-F). Wikipedia lists the genre only as jazz; hard bop is my label. This card replaced "This Here" (Cannonball Adderley) because Cannonball already has Autumn Leaves, Jive Samba and Mercy Mercy Mercy in other files, so a fourth would break the two-card cap. YouTube check: the top hit is the Lou Donaldson Topic upload (6:44, about 565K views). Tier B on view count and the album's standing; it is not on the Grammy Hall of Fame list (A-D page checked).

title: Afro Blue
original_issue: Fantasy 3295 (LP "Cal Tjader's Concert by the Sea", 1959; also listed in discographies as Concert by the Sea, Vol. 1)
personnel: Cal Tjader (vibraphone), Paul Horn (flute), Lonnie Hewitt (piano), Al McKibbon (bass), Willie Bobo (drums, timbales), Mongo Santamaría (percussion, bongos)
trivia: Mongo Santamaría's tune is described as the first jazz standard built on an African 3:2 cross-rhythm, and this live set at Carmel's Sunset Auditorium is its first recorded performance. Santamaría recorded his own composition while playing with Tjader's sextet.

track.title: Afro Blue
track.album: Cal Tjader's Concert by the Sea
track.query: Cal Tjader Sextet Afro Blue Cal Tjader's Concert by the Sea 1959
track.notes: Live take from Sunset Auditorium, Carmel, 20 Apr 1959 (about 6:33), first recorded performance of the tune; not Mongo Santamaría's own Fantasy studio version on "Mongo", John Coltrane's 1963 version or Abbey Lincoln's vocal

notes: Wikipedia's Afro Blue page says the first recorded performance was 20 April 1959 at the Sunset Auditorium, Carmel, with the Cal Tjader Sextet; MusicBrainz dates the recording, lists the personnel above and gives the length (392,986 ms) and the Fantasy 3295 LP number (not cross-checked against a discography; jazzdisco has no Tjader page). Conflict: Wikipedia's text also names Emil Richards (marimba) and Francisco Aguabella (conga) for the first recording, but MusicBrainz does not credit them, so they are left out. The brief suggested a Riverside issue by Mongo Santamaría himself; his own studio version (Fantasy 3291 "Mongo", 1959, 3:58) has no session date or personnel in the sources reached, so this documented live version is used instead.

title: Better Git It in Your Soul
original_issue: Columbia CL 1370 / CS 8171 (LP "Mingus Ah Um", October 1959)
personnel: John Handy (alto sax), Curtis Porter (also known as Shafi Hadi; alto sax), Booker Ervin (tenor sax), Jimmy Knepper (trombone), Horace Parlan (piano), Charles Mingus (bass), Dannie Richmond (drums)
trivia: Mingus built this stomping 6/8 piece on the gospel singing and preaching he heard as a child, and it opens Mingus Ah Um. That album entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2013.

track.title: Better Git It in Your Soul
track.query: Charles Mingus Better Git It in Your Soul Mingus Ah Um 1959
track.notes: Columbia master (matrix CO63154) from 5 May 1959 (7:22), the opening track of Mingus Ah Um; not the 8:30 alternate take on the Legacy Edition or the 1960 Antibes live version

notes: Date, matrix and personnel from jazzdisco (New York, 5 May 1959); jazzdisco names the saxophonist Curtis Porter, while Wikipedia gives Shafi Hadi, who was born William Curtis Porter (Wikipedia's Shafi Hadi page). Instruments by track from Wikipedia's album personnel list: Handy and Hadi on alto, Ervin on tenor, Knepper on trombone. Jazzdisco spells the title "Better Git Hit In Your Soul". Length 7:22 and the gospel inspiration from Wikipedia. Other Mingus cards in the 1955-59 range are Goodbye Pork Pie Hat (part4.js) and Haitian Fight Song (part4b.js), so the two Ah Um cards bring him to four in this part.

title: Fables of Faubus
original_issue: Columbia CL 1370 / CS 8171 (LP "Mingus Ah Um", October 1959)
personnel: John Handy (alto sax), Curtis Porter (also known as Shafi Hadi; tenor sax), Booker Ervin (tenor sax), Jimmy Knepper (trombone), Horace Parlan (piano), Charles Mingus (bass), Dannie Richmond (drums)
trivia: Mingus wrote this satire against Arkansas governor Orval Faubus, who in 1957 used the National Guard to keep nine Black students out of Little Rock Central High School. Columbia refused to release the lyrics, so this album version is instrumental.

track.title: Fables of Faubus
track.query: Charles Mingus Fables of Faubus Mingus Ah Um 1959
track.notes: Instrumental Columbia version from 5 May 1959 (8:14), on Mingus Ah Um; NOT the vocal version "Original Faubus Fables" recorded 20 Oct 1960 for Candid

notes: Date (matrix CO63156) and personnel from jazzdisco; instruments by track from Wikipedia's album page (Handy alto, Hadi tenor, Ervin tenor, Knepper trombone). Length 8:14 is the album page's figure (the song page says 8:13). The lyrics story and the separate Candid vocal recording (20 Oct 1960, "Original Faubus Fables", on Charles Mingus Presents Charles Mingus) are from Wikipedia. Both Mingus cards from this session use the two giant slots the brief allowed me. Note that data/reserve-part4.txt (not loaded by gen.js) also holds records with the same ids (jazz-mingus-fables-of-faubus, jazz-mingus-better-git-it-in-your-soul, jazz-clark-cool-struttin), so they must not be merged from there.

title: Jump, Jive an' Wail
original_issue: Capitol (LP "The Wildest!", 1956; Wikipedia's song and album pages say October 1956, the Louis Prima page says September 1956; catalogue number not checked)
personnel: Louis Prima (vocals, trumpet), Keely Smith (vocals), Sam Butera (tenor sax), James Blount Jr. (trombone), Willie McCumber (piano), Jack Marshall (guitar), Amato Rodrigues (bass), Bobby Morris (drums)
trivia: Prima's wife at the time, Keely Smith, is among the backing singers on this signature number, recorded with Sam Butera and his band. It came back to a mass audience in the late 1990s swing revival, when the Brian Setzer Orchestra covered it.

track.title: Jump, Jive an' Wail
track.query: Louis Prima Jump, Jive an' Wail The Wildest! 1956
track.notes: Prima's original Capitol recording from The Wildest! (3:28), not the Brian Setzer Orchestra's 1998 cover

notes: Wikipedia's song page gives "recorded April 1956", 3:28 and the Capitol label; the album page says the album sessions were 19 and 20 April 1956 (plus 13 Sep 1956 for bonus tracks), so the track is dated to the month only and which of the two April days is not stated. The personnel line is the album-page list for the band (Prima, Smith, Butera and the Witnesses); the sources do not give track-by-track credits, and the song page says only that Keely Smith was one of the backing singers. Conflict on the release month (October vs September 1956); either way the year is 1956. Sources describe the song as jazz swing and jump blues; tier B on its long life, the swing-revival cover and a roughly 500K to 750K view count for the original uploads.

title: Honky Tonk (Parts 1 & 2)
composer: Bill Doggett, Billy Butler, Clifford Scott, Shep Shepherd
original_issue: King two-part 45 rpm single "Honky Tonk" (Part 1 3:05, Part 2 2:32), 1956; catalogue number not checked
personnel: Bill Doggett (organ), Billy Butler (guitar), Clifford Scott (saxophone); the rest of the combo, including co-writer Shep Shepherd, is not itemised in the sources I read
trivia: The two sides of this single spent thirteen non-consecutive weeks at the top of the R&B chart and reached number two on the Billboard Hot 100, making it the biggest R&B hit of 1956. The guitarist Billy Butler, the saxophonist Clifford Scott and Shep Shepherd of Doggett's band share the writing credit with him.

track.title: Honky Tonk (Parts 1 & 2)
track.query: Bill Doggett Honky Tonk Parts 1 and 2 King single 1956
track.notes: The King single, Parts 1 and 2 played back to back (3:05 + 2:32 = 5:37); not the 1972 James Brown version or the many other covers

notes: Wikipedia gives only the year 1956 for the recording (no month, studio or day), so ry is used; the single's catalogue number was not found. Personnel is inferred from the co-writers' own Wikipedia pages: Butler accompanied Doggett in the 1950s, Scott is described as a prominent soloist on "Honky Tonk", and Shepherd worked in Doggett's group and helped write it; no source I read lists the full line-up, so the bassist and drummer are left out. The 5:37 duration is the sum of the two single sides from the song page infobox (the top YouTube hit, 857K views, runs 5:37 and joins both parts). Crossover pick: Wikipedia lists the genre as R&B, jazz and blues, and Doggett is a jazz organist who moved to rhythm and blues; Christgau's Basic Record Library includes it.

title: In Your Own Sweet Way
original_issue: Columbia CL 878 (LP "Brubeck Plays Brubeck", 16 July 1956)
personnel: Dave Brubeck (piano, solo)
trivia: Brubeck made this whole album as solo piano, playing nine of his own compositions over two April days in 1956. It is his own version of a tune that other players have recorded since.

track.title: In Your Own Sweet Way
track.query: Dave Brubeck In Your Own Sweet Way Brubeck Plays Brubeck 1956
track.notes: Solo-piano studio version from Brubeck Plays Brubeck (5:01 on the LP); not the quartet live versions or other players' recordings

notes: Wikipedia's album page says tracks 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8 and 9 (this one is track 3) were recorded on 18 April 1956 and tracks 4 and 6 on 19 April; jazzdisco lists "Dave Brubeck Solo" at NYC, 18 and 19 April 1956 and gives Columbia CL 878. Conflict: Wikipedia's infobox gives the place as Brubeck's house in Oakland, jazzdisco says New York City; the card does not use the place. Length 5:01 from the album page track list (the Topic upload runs 4:58). The trivia's remark that other players have recorded the tune is general knowledge, not taken from a source page, so it is phrased loosely. With Take Five, Blue Rondo a la Turk and Unsquare Dance, this is Brubeck's fourth card in the set.

title: Every Day I Have the Blues
original_issue: Clef MG C-678 (LP "Count Basie Swings, Joe Williams Sings", 1955)
personnel: Joe Williams (vocals), Count Basie (piano), Wendell Culley, Reunald Jones, Thad Jones, Joe Newman (trumpets), Henry Coker, Bill Hughes, Benny Powell (trombones), Marshall Royal and Bill Graham (alto sax), Frank Wess (alto and tenor sax, flute), Frank Foster (tenor sax), Charlie Fowlkes (baritone sax), Freddie Green (guitar), Eddie Jones (bass), Sonny Payne (drums); arranger Ernie Wilkins
trivia: This album was Joe Williams's debut as the featured singer with the Basie band, and its opening track is a slow blues. AllMusic gives the album five stars and calls the debut a landmark moment.

track.title: Every Day I Have the Blues
track.album: Count Basie Swings, Joe Williams Sings
track.query: Count Basie Joe Williams Every Day I Have the Blues Count Basie Swings, Joe Williams Sings 1955
track.notes: Clef studio recording from 17 May 1955 (5:29 on the LP), not Basie and Williams's later live or remade versions or the Pinetop Sparks or Memphis Slim originals

notes: Wikipedia's album page gives Fine Sound, New York, 17 May 1955 for tracks 1 to 4 (this is track 1) and 26 July 1955 for tracks 5 to 9, the 5:29 length, the arranger credit (Ernie Wilkins on tracks 1 and 6) and the personnel list for the album as a whole; no discography page was available for the band, so the personnel is the album-level list. The composer credit is the album page's (Peter Chapman, Mayall York); the song page documents Pinetop Sparks's 1935 original and Memphis Slim's 1949 rework. Replaces Basie's 1939 Kansas City Seven "Lester Leaps In" in the set so that Basie stays at five cards. The YouTube hit for this version has about 136K views.

title: Twisted
original_issue: Columbia (LP "The Hottest New Group in Jazz", December 1959; catalogue number not checked)
personnel: Dave Lambert, Jon Hendricks and Annie Ross (vocals), backed by the Ike Isaacs Trio (Ike Isaacs, bass; Gildo Mahones, piano; the album lists several drummers)
trivia: Annie Ross wrote the lyrics in 1952 to a tenor-saxophone solo that Wardell Gray had recorded in 1949, and the lyric makes fun of psychoanalysis. The trio, backed by the Ike Isaacs Trio, put the song on their fourth album.

track.title: Twisted
track.album: The Hottest New Group in Jazz
track.query: Lambert, Hendricks & Ross Twisted The Hottest New Group in Jazz 1959
track.notes: The trio's Columbia version (2:19), not Annie Ross's 1952 Prestige original, Wardell Gray's 1949 instrumental or the Joni Mitchell and Bette Midler covers

notes: The album page gives December 1959 as the release and says the group is backed by the Ike Isaacs Trio, but gives no session date. The 1959 recording year is therefore inferred from the December 1959 release; no source I reached dates the session. Personnel: the album page says the group is backed by the Ike Isaacs Trio and lists the album's musicians as a whole (several bassists and drummers, plus Harry Edison and Pony Poindexter on other tracks); Isaacs is the trio's namesake bassist and Mahones the only pianist listed, but which drummer plays on this track is not stated. Annie Ross's own 1952 original (9 Oct 1952, NYC, Prestige 794 per jazzdisco) is a different recording that is not on the card. Ross herself has this one card in the set.

title: The Late, Late Show
original_issue: Capitol (LP "The Late, Late Show", 1957; catalogue number not checked)
personnel: Dakota Staton (vocals) with an orchestra that the sources I found do not name
trivia: The title song was Staton's biggest hit, and the album that carries it was her debut. The album was recorded over two sessions, on 28 February and 2 March 1957.

track.title: The Late, Late Show
track.query: Dakota Staton The Late, Late Show The Late, Late Show 1957
track.notes: Capitol album version (2:34); not Staton's later remakes or the live versions

notes: Wikipedia's album page gives recording dates of 28 February and 2 March 1957 (so both fall in 1957) and a 1957 release on Capitol; which date the title song was cut is not stated, so ry is used. The track length 2:34 is from the album page track list; the YouTube Topic uploads run about 2:33 to 2:37. AllMusic (quoted on the album page) says the orchestra is largely unidentified, so no personnel is listed. The title song is a hit single but this is a single-source card; the tier rests on the roughly 155K to 158K views of the two best uploads and its status as her signature song.

title: Blue Sands
original_issue: Pacific Jazz PJ-1209 / ST-20143 (LP "Chico Hamilton Quintet featuring Buddy Collette", 1956; reissued as "Spectacular!")
personnel: Chico Hamilton (drums), Buddy Collette (tenor sax, alto sax, flute, clarinet), Fred Katz (cello), Jim Hall (guitar), Carson Smith (bass)
trivia: Hamilton's quintet had a cellist, Fred Katz, and a multi-reed player, Buddy Collette, instead of a trumpet and a pianist. AllMusic's Scott Yanow calls it a chamber jazz unit that hinted at classical music, and Collette wrote "Blue Sands".

track.title: Blue Sands
track.album: Chico Hamilton Quintet featuring Buddy Collette
track.query: Chico Hamilton Quintet Blue Sands Chico Hamilton Quintet featuring Buddy Collette 1955
track.notes: Pacific Jazz album version from August 1955 (6:30), not the later re-recordings

notes: Wikipedia's album page gives recording dates of 4 and 23 August 1955, with one side live (The Strollers, Long Beach) and the other recorded in the studio (Radio Recorders, Hollywood); it does not say which date or side holds "Blue Sands", so only the month is used. No discography (jazzdisco has no Hamilton page) was reachable to settle it. Personnel and the 6:30 length are from the album page; the Yanow quote is from the album page's reception section. Tier C on view counts (about 74K and 26K on the best uploads): a fan landmark of chamber jazz, included for the style spread; this is the one recording of the quintet in the set.

title: Parchman Farm
original_issue: Prestige PRLP 7121 (LP "Local Color", 1958)
personnel: Mose Allison (piano, vocals), Addison Farmer (bass), Nick Stabulas (drums)
trivia: This is the first recording of Allison's own "Parchman Farm", which shares only its title with Bukka White's 1940 blues of the same name. John Mayall's Bluesbreakers later covered it on their album with Eric Clapton.

track.title: Parchman Farm
track.query: Mose Allison Parchman Farm Local Color 1957
track.notes: Studio trio version from Local Color (3:17), not Bukka White's 1940 song or the many covers

notes: Date (8 Nov 1957), Van Gelder Studio (Hackensack), Prestige PRLP 7121, the 1958 release, personnel and 3:17 length from Wikipedia's album page; the album page lists trumpet by Allison on a different track. The song page and Mose Allison's page document that the song is an original unrelated to White's, was his most requested song for two decades, and was covered by John Mayall. Style label hard-bop is a rough fit (Wikipedia lists the album as blues and jazz); there is no blues or vocal-jazz style in the enum. Roughly 99K views on the best upload, so tier B rather than A.

title: The Train and the River
original_issue: Atlantic LP 1254 (LP "The Jimmy Giuffre 3", 1957); Atlantic EP 604 (1957)
personnel: Jimmy Giuffre (clarinet), Jim Hall (guitar), Ralph Peña (bass)

title: Pithecanthropus Erectus
original_issue: Atlantic LP 1237 (LP "Pithecanthropus Erectus", August 1956)
personnel: Jackie McLean (alto sax), J. R. Monterose (tenor sax), Mal Waldron (piano), Charles Mingus (bass), Willie Jones (drums)
trivia: Mingus described this ten-minute tone poem as the rise of humankind from its early ancestors to a downfall caused by greed and the oppression of others. It was the first album on which he taught his musicians their parts by ear rather than writing out the chords.

title: Mack the Knife
composer: Kurt Weill, Bertolt Brecht, Marc Blitzstein (English lyrics)
original_issue: Atco (LP "That's All", March 1959); Atco single "Mack the Knife" b/w "Was There a Call for Me", August 1959 (single edit 3:04; catalogue number not checked)
personnel: Bobby Darin (vocals), Richard Wess (arranger, conductor), Doc Severinsen (trumpet), with a studio orchestra; the drummer and bassist are credited differently by two Wikipedia pages (see notes)
trivia: Darin cut his swinging version of Kurt Weill's Threepenny Opera song in about three takes, raising the key a semitone with each verse from the third on. He was reluctant to release it as a single, but it reached number one in the US and won the Grammy for Record of the Year.

notes: Wikipedia's song page (Bobby Darin section and infobox) and the album page agree on the recording date, 19 December 1958, the Atco single in August 1959 (3:04) and the album length 3:10 (the song page infobox says 3:11 for the album version); the album page dates the LP to March 1959, so the album came out before the single. Conflict on the rhythm section: the song page names Don Lamond (drums) and Milt Hinton (bass) for this song, while the album page lists Osie Johnson (drums on "Mack the Knife"), Don Lamond (drums) and Eddie Safranski (bass), with Hank Jones on piano and Barry Galbraith on guitar for the album; the card therefore lists only the leader, arranger and Doc Severinsen, who both pages agree on. The key-change and take-count detail is from the song page. Ella Fitzgerald's 1960 Berlin live version is another card in the set, so this is the second version of the song (Armstrong's 1955 version is not a card). Crossover pick: Wikipedia lists the genre as traditional pop, jazz and lounge; tier A as one of the best-known recordings of the era. YouTube check: the first hits for a plain query are the Ed Sullivan Show TV clip and uploads of the 3:04 single edit (the official Darin channel upload has about 7.4M views), so the query adds "official audio" and the label.
